items.claim: A subdomain takeover is established when a hostname's CNAME still points at a third-party PaaS domain that no longer serves, letting the tester register that third-party hostname and take control of the subdomain.
items.body:
A subdomain takeover is established when a hostname's CNAME still points at a third-party PaaS domain that no longer serves, letting the tester register that third-party hostname and take control of the subdomain.

HackTricks reference: easy methods (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/subdomain-takeover/easy_methods.md)
items.disproof: The CNAME target still serves content or returns a provider-owned response other than a dangling 404, meaning the subscription is active and the hostname is unclaimable.

sources.quote:
1:Grab all subdomains of target. i.e, subfinder -d flaws.cloud | tee -a domains.txt
 
2:Run this one liner
 
3:cat domains.txt | while read domain;do dig $domain;done | tee -a digs.txt
 
4::Grab all the CNAME Entries i.e, cat digs.txt | grep CNAME
 
5:Find a domain that is pointed to third party domain like sub.exampple.com CNAME x.aws.com
 
6:Check wheather the main subdomain is down
 
7:Go to host provider where the domain is pointed to and register that domain if you registered congrats you have takeover the subdomain.

items.claim: A dangling record that enables takeover can be a CNAME or an A record pointing at third-party services, so DNS enumeration has to inspect both record types instead of CNAMEs alone.
items.body:

items.claim: A taken-over subdomain is dangerous beyond content control because the attacker's service can inherit the domain owner's wildcard SSL, making phishing on the subdomain TLS-trusted and unknown to the owner.

items.claim: A subdomain becomes attacker-controllable when a cancelled third-party service leaves its CNAME behind in the DNS zone, so the dangling record rather than the provider account is what has to be removed.
items.body:
A subdomain becomes attacker-controllable when a cancelled third-party service leaves its CNAME behind in the DNS zone, so the dangling record rather than the provider account is what has to be removed.

HackTricks reference: subdomain takeover (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/subdomain-takeover/subdomain_takeover.md)
items.disproof: The CNAME is deleted from the zone file, or the hostname no longer resolves to the abandoned third-party service.

sources.quote:
These subdomains use a CNAME record to another domain \[eg. xyz.company.com CNAME xyz.cloudservice.com]
* Now due to whatever reason, the company decides to stop utilizing this service and to save some bucks, the company cancels the subscription of the 3rd party cloud service provider.
* But, the company forgets to update or simply remove the CNAME record in the DNS zone file
* Since the CNAME record is not deleted from company.com DNS zone, anyone who registers xyz.cloudservice.com has full control over xyz.company.com until the DNS record is present.
